title: How Gold Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore gold: its history as a prized metal from ancient Egypt, Nubia, Bulgaria and the Maya/Aztec/Inca worlds through the Greek and Roman minting of coins, Croesus of Lydia, Marco Polo and Columbus-era gold lust (El Dorado, Brazil's Minas Gerais), the gold rushes in North Carolina, California, Australia and South Africa, how gold is prospected, mined (load and placer deposits, open pit and underground), extracted via crushing, cyanide leaching, electrowinning and smelting, refined into ingots, alloyed into carats (white, red gold), used in jewelry, electronics, NASA and dentistry, the gold standard and Fort Knox, and the environmental damage of mining and illegal mercury gold mining in Guiana. The episode ends with a listener mail from Professor Tom about life lessons from the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mayan and Aztec gold lore
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the show's name and a January history tidbit about the Maya conquest of Tikal. They discuss Aztec names for gold and the Egyptians' view of gold as divine, and Nubia as an early gold-mining area.

segments.title: Gold statistics
segments.summary: Gold stats: about 161,000 tons ever mined, compared with aluminum output, and about 15 percent of gold ever found is unaccounted for. Gold's malleability is noted: one ounce can be drawn into a 50-mile wire or hammered to a thin sheet.

segments.title: Early gold use and the first coins
segments.summary: Gold working dates to around 4000 BC in Bulgaria, Egypt used gold as near-currency, and Croesus of Lydia is credited as the first to mint gold coins. Greeks and Romans followed, and South American cultures such as the Inca worked gold into masks, chalices and gold leaf.

segments.title: Explorers, Marco Polo and El Dorado
segments.summary: European gold lust is traced through Marco Polo, who reportedly inspired Columbus. King Ferdinand's instruction to get gold 'at all hazards' is cited, and the myth of El Dorado drove conquistadors. Brazil's Minas Gerais became the largest gold producer by 1720 using slave labor.

segments.title: Gold rushes in North Carolina, California and Australia
segments.summary: North Carolina was the first American gold rush and supplied the US Mint until the 1830s. The California gold rush is discussed, along with Australia's gold rush after discoveries in New South Wales in the 1850s.

segments.title: South Africa and modern gold production
segments.summary: South Africa is named as the leading gold producer today, followed by the United States, with Nevada the top US producer.

segments.title: Prospecting and mining methods
segments.summary: Prospecting is explained, from old luck-based searches to modern equipment and drilling samples. Load deposits are mined by open pit or underground shafts with explosives, while placer deposits are panned from streams and beaches.

segments.title: Gold extraction and refining process
segments.summary: Ore is crushed and ground with steel balls, then leached with cyanide in a slurry, with gold adsorbing to carbon. It is stripped with a caustic solution, recovered by electrowinning, smelted into dore bars, and refined with soda ash and borax to about 99.9 percent purity as ingots.

segments.title: Heist movies, Fort Knox and gold price
segments.summary: Hosts discuss gold ingot weight (27 pounds) in Die Hard 3 and Fort Knox storage, with a rough worth of about 25.6 billion dollars at the older price. They talk about why gold is hoarded and the price rise after the economic downturn.

segments.title: Gold alloys, carats and uses
segments.summary: Gold is alloyed into white gold and red gold. Carat ratings differ by country: 14 carat in the US, 22 in India, 18 in Europe. About two thirds of gold goes to jewelry. Gold's conductivity and corrosion resistance make it used in electronics, NASA's Space Shuttle Columbia, and gold film, and in dental crowns, compared with the silver fish fork.

segments.title: Gold standard, asteroids and environmental damage
segments.summary: The gold standard (1900 to 1971) is mentioned, with the US abandoning it for fiat currency. Asteroid gold is raised. Mining environmental harm is discussed, including roughly 250 tons of ore per ounce, cyanide runoff, and illegal gold mining with mercury in Guiana, citing a Harper's article by Damon Tabor.

segments.title: Listener mail from Professor Tom
segments.summary: A community college communications professor shares life lessons he sees in the show. The hosts close with a note about the Chuck-and-Josh mail and show contact info.
